newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Will coffee rally start boom/bust cycle?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Will coffee rally start boom/bust cycle?.

text.p: A recent rally in world arabica coffee prices may encourage growers to boost output but may also dampen consumption to the extent that more supply could become too much, analysts said.
"It's a very fine line between incentivising production and disincentivising consumption," said Michael McDougall, director of commodities futures at Fimat Futures in Sao Paulo.

Prices of arabica coffee futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange have risen more than 70 percent since mid-December due to a number of factors including concern over crops in Colombia and Brazil.
However, 190 cents a lb in the first contract month is still a long way away from the spike to 263.50 seen in July 1994 after two sudden frosts ravaged many Brazil trees.
While production suffered the following year, retail prices rose swiftly, stifling consumer demand, and coffee bean prices actually returned to pre-frost levels by July 1995.
The boom/bust cycle was surprisingly swift, giving growers little reason to invest in production.
"I thought we would see an increase in production because of the high prices after the frost in 1994. But the prices rallied and then came quickly off again," McDougall said.

Producers were doubly wary about increasing investments with fresh memory of prices as low as 48.10 cents a lb in 1992 and 1993 due to a rush of supply after an international export quota agreement collapsed in 1989.

Roasters in consuming countries used the fat years to build up stocks which at one point reached over 20 million 60-kg bags. Only now have they have been reduced to what producers see as acceptable levels of around eight million bags.

Producers themselves are well aware the time has come to invest in increasing output given world coffee production in 1996/97 (October/September) is estimated to reach around 97 million bags against consumption of about 99 million bags.
At the same time they also realise they have to ensure more production does not become over production.

"Since 1989, there has been zero long-term investment in coffee except for Vietnam. We are concerned that if we do not do something there will be a supply problem in the short and the medium-term," said Herbert de Sola, El Salvador's representative to the Association of Coffee Producing Countries.
"But we want reliable supply, not excessive supply," he added.
KEY PRODUCER PLANS MERELY TO RESTORE FALLING OUTPUT
For producers to begin investing in more production, prices would have to stay in a range of 160 to 180 cents a lb for at least a year to see higher output, McDougall said.
But at the same time he and other analysts do not see huge short to medium-term potential in growth from the world's two largest producers - Brazil and Colombia.

Brazil's stated goal is merely to see national output at an average of between 30 and 35 million bags in the next 10 years. This is far from sensationalist given that in the past it has produced in excess of 40 million bags.

Its coming crop is seen at around 20 million bags by domestic producers and nearer to 23 million bags by Brazilian traders. But this is unexpectedly small after many overseas had been anticipating a harvest nearer to 30 million bags allowing for a normal recovery from the 1994 frosts.

Producers already have an eye on the 1998/99 crop which could bounce back to 30 million bags but there is some concern over premature blossoms on parts of branches which would normally only be blossoming in October for next year's harvest.

"Right now the potential of Brazilian production in the next two to three years is up to 33 million bags," said Leon Yallouz, formerly a forecaster for the U.S. Department of Agriculture and now a private consultant.
"That is working on the potential of coffee trees currently in the ground and those trees planted recently," he added.
In Colombia, likewise, the aim is more to restore output to levels achieved in previous years.

Recently the head of Colombia's National Coffee Federation recently said that the federation was determined to lift production back up to average annual output of 13 million 60-kg bags from a forecasted 10.4 million bags in 1996/97.
HOW MUCH WILL SHOPPERS PAY FOR THEIR JAR OF COFFEE?
Producers for the time being therefore look as if they will seek to ensure there is no repeat of the glut in supply seen in the early 1990s but what they cannot control is consumption.
Recent forecasts are that world demand could grow to 108 million bags by the year 2000.

But these projections may change if retail prices rise to the extent consumers think twice about making a pot of coffee and throwing what they do not drink down the sink as happened when prices in the shops rose after the frost rally.
"The coffee trade's best friend used to be the sink but that all ended after the frosts and I think the same thing will happen again," said John Wolthers of Santos exporters Icatu/Sumatra.
Already some German, French and U.S. roasters have raised retail prices because of the recent rally in green bean prices.

In Brazil, some domestic roasters have increased prices by 30 to 50 percent in recent weeks and the impact is already been felt on consumption, said David Nahum, secretary-general of the Brazilian Coffee Industry Association which represents roasters.
The question is what price can producers hope to achieve which will not cause roasters to put up retail prices to a level too bitter for consumers' tastes.

"In order to avoid the boom-bust cycle, producers need to see consumption grow sharply over the next few years. And to do this, prices need to remain reasonable," said Lawrence Eagles, analyst at London brokers GNI.
"A world price of between 130 and 150 cents a lb is probably the maximum that producers can hope to receive without seriously detracting from global coffee consumption growth," he added.
PRODUCERS ALSO HAVE TO THINK ABOUT HOW TO SELL STOCKS
One other factor to be taken into consideration is how producers will manage their stocks, particularly in the two key countries Brazil and Colombia.
The Brazilian government, which currently has a stockpile of around 13 million bags, has already embarked on a monthly sale program of small quantities to ensure internal supply.

In Colombia, a top federation official recently said stocks totalled around six million bags of which "the majority is still in excellent condition" and that the federation also intended to draw on stocks to make up for a smaller crop.
The rate and quantity in which these stocks are liquidated will determine the world price for coffee over the next 18 months, Eagles said.

"The best option for the future would be if the governments sold a large proportion of their stockpiles and pushed the price down towards a dollar a lb. This, we have seen over the past two years, causes a very rapid increase in coffee consumption," he said.
"The worst case scenario would be a sharp rise in coffee prices and falling consumption. And this we are in danger of seeing at the moment," he added.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
